one_liner: Go package with AVX2 assembly multi-byte, class, ASCII and substring scans on []byte; beats bytes.ContainsAny, bytes.Index and its own SWAR loops above 64 bytes.
what_it_does: Package github.com/gofiber/utils/v2/simd provides byte-search and validation functions on []byte. Memchr2 and Memchr3 return the first index of any of two or three bytes. MemchrPair finds two bytes at a fixed distance. MemchrDigit, MemchrWord and MemchrNotWord scan for byte classes. IsASCII, FirstNonASCII and CountNonASCII validate ASCII, and Memmem returns a substring index with bytes.Index semantics. There is no single-byte Memchr, because bytes.IndexByte is already vectorised. Fiber's top-level generic helpers (utils.IsASCII, IndexAny2, IndexAny3) route string or []byte inputs of 32 bytes or more into it on amd64.
how_it_is_fast: Each AVX2 kernel (Go assembly) handles four 32-byte vectors per iteration. It ORs the four compare masks so a 128-byte block costs one VPMOVMSKB and one branch, and finishes with an overlapping last vector instead of a scalar tail. The word-class test uses two VPSHUFB nibble-table lookups, and the digit test is one biased VPADDB plus one compare. CountNonASCII accumulates per-lane counts in byte lanes and flushes them through VPSADBW. Memmem is a rare-byte prefilter in the style of BurntSushi's memchr: SelectRareBytes ranks needle bytes with a fixed frequency table. Needles of 2-6 bytes are scanned with MemchrPair for their two rarest bytes at the exact distance, and longer needles with bytes.IndexByte for the rarest byte; the search falls back to bytes.Index after 16 failed verifications.
when_to_use: Go services on amd64 with AVX2 that scan []byte payloads of hundreds of bytes to a few KiB for any of 2-3 delimiters, digits, \w or non-\w bytes, or non-ASCII bytes, for example HTTP header and query parsing in Fiber.
Replacing bytes.ContainsAny or bytes.IndexAny with a 2-3 byte ASCII set on inputs of 64 bytes or more. At 512 B the README shows 4.2 ns vs 214 ns.

Substring search with short needles (2-6 bytes, two distinct values) on 65+ byte haystacks where the needle's bytes are rare in the data: 96 B 8.3 vs 20.1 ns, 4 KiB 38 vs 922 ns against bytes.Contains.
ASCII validation or counting non-ASCII bytes on inputs above 64 B: IsASCII 4 KiB 14.2 vs 46.7 ns, CountNonASCII 17.4 vs 145.3 ns against the SWAR fallback.
when_not_to_use: Inputs under about 64 bytes. Below 32 B the kernels never run, and the exported call is slower than the fallback it dispatches to (IsASCII 8 B 2.11 vs 0.95 ns, MemchrPair 8 B 5.21 vs 2.53 ns scalar). At 32-64 B, IsASCII, MemchrPair and Memmem are level or behind.
Non-amd64 targets (arm64 and others) or CPUs without AVX2. Only SWAR fallbacks run there, with no NEON or SVE kernels.

Memmem on data where the needle's 'rare' bytes are common, such as digits in numeric logs, high bytes in non-Latin UTF-8, or long needles anchored on frequent letters. The prefilter then exhausts its 16-miss budget and tracks bytes.Index: the README's single-rare-byte rows trail it (4 KiB 922.7 vs 863.5 ns), and the adversarial case is at parity (1.033 ms both).
Single-byte search, or repeated searches for one needle. There is no Memchr (use bytes.IndexByte), and Memmem recomputes SelectRareBytes on every call; it has no prebuilt searcher.
Projects on Go older than 1.26, since go.mod declares go 1.26.0.

integration.dependencies: golang.org/x/sys/cpu for AVX2/POPCNT detection, plus the module's own swar package; the utils/v2 module as a whole also requires fxamacker/cbor, google/uuid and shamaton/msgpack
integration.platforms: amd64 with AVX2 for the kernels (CountNonASCII also needs POPCNT); portable SWAR fallback on every other GOARCH
integration.thread_safety: Stateless functions on caller slices. The CPU flags are read once at package init, and the frequency table is unexported and read-only, so concurrent use is safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Memmem returns the same index as bytes.Index (fuzzed against it), so it can replace bytes.Index or bytes.Contains on []byte. Memchr2 and Memchr3 take byte arguments rather than bytes.IndexAny's UTF-8 chars string, so they match it only for ASCII sets. Package simd has no string variants; the top-level utils generics cover strings.

gotchas: The headline 60x (Memchr2) and 46x (Memchr3) are measured against bytes.ContainsAny, a per-byte set loop. The rows labelled 'scalar' are actually the package's own 8-byte SWAR word loops (memchr2Generic uses swar.ZeroLanes), not byte loops: 16x and 14x at 4 KiB. The fairer stdlib idiom, two vectorised bytes.IndexByte passes, is not benchmarked.

Benchmark harness (simd/bench_test.go): results are checked, so calls are not optimised away. But every row reuses one warm buffer of at most 4 KiB, only full-scan misses are timed, and the table is one -count=1 run on an unnamed 'AMD EPYC' with GOMAXPROCS=4. The README says small rows drifted up to 17% between runs. The Memmem needle "q7z" has two bytes that never occur in the 'a'..'w' haystack, which is the best case for the paired prefilter. The 4 KiB IsASCII row (14.17 ns, about 289 bytes/ns) is L1 load bandwidth, not memory bandwidth.

A latent out-of-bounds read existed in the AVX2 count kernel. Commit 21ac610 (2026-07-29) fixed countNonASCIIAVX2's loop test (base < end instead of base <= end-32), which could read up to 24 bytes past a 40-byte slice and SIGSEGV at a page end. The only caller masked the length, so the tests missed it. A Test_KernelsAreSelfBounding guard and POPCNT gating were added, and fuzz targets compare every exported function against references and bytes.Index.

The README explains a 10% MemchrPair swing as Intel's Skylake JCC-erratum effect and pins block loops with a BLOCKALIGN macro, but the published runs are on an AMD EPYC. Code alignment still moves results, so treat small deltas between builds as noise.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only Go entry in this category for multi-byte memchr, class scans and memmem; sliceslice (Rust AVX2 substring search), memx-cdy (Rust memchr/memmem behind a C ABI) and WojciechMula's toys strstr (C++) serve other languages. Pick it in Go amd64 code that already depends on Fiber or wants vectorised IndexAny-style and ASCII scans without cgo; for single-byte search stay with bytes.IndexByte.
verified_claims_summary: The README's single go test -count=1 run on linux/amd64 'AMD EPYC' (GOMAXPROCS 4, Go 1.26+, warm 8 B-4 KiB buffers, full-scan misses) shows the following. Memmem: 38.44 vs 921.5 ns for bytes.Contains at 4 KiB (24x) and 10.22 vs 119.8 ns at 512 B, but slower than bytes.Contains up to 64 B (8 B 4.45 vs 3.55 ns). Memchr2: 26.22 ns vs 422.0 ns for the SWAR loop (16x) and 1572 ns for bytes.ContainsAny (60x) at 4 KiB. ASCII scans at 4 KiB against the SWAR fallback: IsASCII 14.17 vs 46.72 ns (3.3x), FirstNonASCII 14.19 vs 108.7 ns (7.7x), CountNonASCII 17.36 vs 145.3 ns (8.4x). Ratios are derived from page data.
